label: s
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{s}
Let $ s $ be a function from $ \mathcal{P} $ into the power set of $\mathcal{T}$ (understood as the set of topics or `subject-matters'). Then $s$ is extended to
formulas and sets of formulas by the following clauses:
\begin{itemize}\itemsep=0pt
	\item $s(A)=\bigcup_{p\in\mathrm{var}(A)}s(p)$, 
	\item $s(\Gamma)=\bigcup_{A\in\Gamma}s(A)$.
\end{itemize}	
A valuation, relative to $s$, is a function $v_s$ from $\mathcal{P}$ into the set of truth
values $\{1, 0\}$. The valuation $v_s$ of formulas is defined for negation, conjunction, and disjunction,
as in classical logic. For implication, $v_s$ is defined as follows (several options are possible):
\begin{enumerate}\itemsep=0pt
	\item $ v_s(A\rightarrow B)=1 $ iff \big($v_s(A)=0$ or $v_s(B)=1$\big) and $ s(B)\subseteq s(A)$,
	\item $ v_s(A\rightarrow B)=1 $ iff \big($v_s(A)=0$ or $v_s(B)=1$\big) and $ s(A)\subseteq s(B)$,
	\item $ v_s(A\rightarrow B)=1 $ iff \big($v_s(A)=0$ or $v_s(B)=1$\big) and $ s(A)=s(B)$.
\end{enumerate}
For a given function $s$, a formula $A$ is $s$-valid iff
$v_s(A)=1$ for every valuation $v_s$.

title: Definition
body_md:
An element $i\in V$ is an infectious value of a logical matrix $\langle V,C,D\rangle$ iff for every $n$-ary function $c\in C$ and every tuple
$\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\rangle\in V^n$, if $x_j=i$ for some $1\leq j\leq n$,
then $c(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=i$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: A logic having a logical matrix with an infectious value is said to be infectious.

title: \textbf{Theorem}
body_md:
Let $\mathbf{L}$ be the logic determined by the matrix
$\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{L}}=\langle V,C,D\rangle$, and let $i\notin V$.
Assume that every function in $C$ has positive finite arity. For every
$k$-ary function $c\in C$, let $c^{i}$ be the $k$-ary function on
$V\cup\{i\}$ defined by $c^{i}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})=i$ if
$x_{j}=i$ for some $1\leq j\leq k$, and
$c^{i}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})=c(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})$ otherwise.
Let $C^{i}=\{c^{i}:c\in C\}$. Let $\mathbf{S}$ and $\mathbf{T}$ be the logics determined by the
matrices $\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{S}}=\langle V\cup\{i\},C^{i},D\rangle$
and $\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{T}}=\langle V\cup\{i\},C^{i},D\cup\{i\}\rangle$, respectively. Then:
\begin{itemize}\itemsep=0pt
    \item $\Gamma\models_{\mathbf{S}}\Delta$ iff there is some
    $\Delta'\subseteq\Delta$ such that
    $\operatorname{var}(\Delta')\subseteq\operatorname{var}(\Gamma)$
    and $\Gamma\models_{\mathbf{L}}\Delta'$;

    \item $\Gamma\models_{\mathbf{T}}\Delta$ iff there is some
    $\Gamma'\subseteq\Gamma$ such that
    $\operatorname{var}(\Gamma')\subseteq\operatorname{var}(\Delta)$
    and $\Gamma'\models_{\mathbf{L}}\Delta$.
\end{itemize}

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) Follows from the fact that $ \not\models p_1\vee\neg p_1$ under the valuation $ v $ such that $ v(p_1)=\nicefrac[]{1}{2} $.
	
	(2)	Let $v(p)=\nicefrac[]{1}{2}$ for every propositional variable $p$.
A straightforward induction on formulas shows that $v(A)=\nicefrac[]{1}{2}$
for every formula $A$. Since $\nicefrac[]{1}{2}$ is not designated in
$\bf K_3^d$, the logic has no tautologies.
	
	(3) Follows from the fact that $p_1,\neg p_1\not\models p_2$ under the valuation $ v $ such that $ v(p_1)=\nicefrac[]{1}{2} $ and $ v(p_2)=0 $.	

(4) We adopt Epstein's proof \cite{Epstein} of the fact that
\textbf{LP} and \textbf{CL} have the same set of tautologies.\footnote{This
result was first obtained by Martin \cite{Martin}.} Let us prove that a formula $F$ is not valid in \textbf{CL} iff there is a valuation $v$ in $\bf LP^d$ such that $v(F)=0$. Observe that $(\ast_1)$ any valuation in \textbf{CL} can also be regarded
as a valuation in $\bf LP^d$. Thus, $(\ast_2)$ if, under some
classical valuation $v'$, we have $v'(F)=0$, then we also have
$v'(F)=0$ in $\bf LP^d$.

Conversely, suppose that there is a valuation $v$ in $\bf LP^d$
such that $v(F)=0$. Let us define a valuation $w$ in \textbf{CL} as
follows. For any $p\in\mathcal{P}$, let $w(p)=1$ iff
$v(p)\in\{1,\nicefrac[]{1}{2}\}$, and let $w(p)=0$ iff $v(p)=0$. By structural
induction on $A$, it is possible to show that:
\begin{enumerate}\itemsep=0pt
    \item[(a)] if $v(A)=0$, then $w(A)=0$;
    \item[(b)] if $v(A)=1$, then $w(A)=1$.
\end{enumerate}

We prove (a) and (b) simultaneously by induction on the complexity of
$A$. As an example, we consider the case of implication. Suppose that
$A=B\rightarrow C$. By the induction hypothesis, $v(B)=0$ implies
$w(B)=0$, $v(C)=0$ implies $w(C)=0$, $v(B)=1$ implies $w(B)=1$, and
$v(C)=1$ implies $w(C)=1$.

Assume that $v(B\rightarrow C)=0$. Then $v(B)=1$ and $v(C)=0$. Hence,
by the induction hypothesis, $w(B)=1$ and $w(C)=0$. Therefore,
$w(B\rightarrow C)=0$. Thus, $v(B\rightarrow C)=0$ implies
$w(B\rightarrow C)=0$.

Assume that $v(B\rightarrow C)=1$. Then either
$v(B)=1$ and $v(C)=1$, or $v(B)=0$ and $v(C)=1$, or $v(B)=0$ and
$v(C)=0$. Suppose first that $v(B)=1$ and $v(C)=1$. By the induction
hypothesis, $w(B)=1$ and $w(C)=1$. Hence, $w(B\rightarrow C)=1$.
Suppose next that $v(B)=0$ and $v(C)=1$. By the induction hypothesis,
$w(B)=0$ and $w(C)=1$. Thus, $w(B\rightarrow C)=1$. Finally, suppose
that $v(B)=0$ and $v(C)=0$. By the induction hypothesis, $w(B)=0$ and
$w(C)=0$. Consequently, $w(B\rightarrow C)=1$. Therefore,
$v(B\rightarrow C)=1$ implies $w(B\rightarrow C)=1$.

The remaining cases are similar. Since $v(F)=0$, condition (a) yields
$w(F)=0$. Hence, $\not\models_{\mathbf{CL}}F$.

body_md:
The following rules are height-preserving admissible in \textbf{BSC}:
    \begin{center}
        \noindent\begin{tabular}{ll}	
	$(\mathord{W}\mathord{\Rightarrow\mid})$ \ $\dfrac{\Gamma
		\Rightarrow \Delta \mid S}{A, \Gamma \Rightarrow \Delta \mid S}$ &
	$(\mathord{\Rightarrow}\mathord{W\mid})$ \ $\dfrac{\Gamma
		\Rightarrow \Delta \mid S}{\Gamma
		\Rightarrow \Delta, A \mid S}$\\[16pt]
	
	$(\mathord{\mid W}\mathord{\Rightarrow})$ \ $\dfrac{S \mid \Pi\Rightarrow\Sigma}{S\mid A, \Pi\Rightarrow\Sigma}$ &
	$(\mathord{\mid\Rightarrow}\mathord{W})$ \ $\dfrac{S \mid \Pi\Rightarrow\Sigma}{S \mid \Pi\Rightarrow\Sigma, A}$\\[16pt]	
\end{tabular}
\noindent\begin{tabular}{ll}	
	$(\mathord{C}\mathord{\Rightarrow\mid})$ \ $\dfrac{A,A,\Gamma
		\Rightarrow \Delta \mid S}{A, \Gamma \Rightarrow \Delta \mid S}$ &
	$(\mathord{\Rightarrow}\mathord{C\mid})$ \ $\dfrac{\Gamma
		\Rightarrow \Delta, A, A \mid S}{\Gamma
		\Rightarrow \Delta, A \mid S}$\\[16pt]
	
	$(\mathord{\mid C}\mathord{\Rightarrow})$ \ $\dfrac{S \mid A,A, \Pi\Rightarrow\Sigma}{S\mid A, \Pi\Rightarrow\Sigma}$ &
	$(\mathord{\mid\Rightarrow}\mathord{C})$ \ $\dfrac{S \mid \Pi\Rightarrow\Sigma, A, A}{S \mid \Pi\Rightarrow\Sigma, A}$\\[16pt]

label: Invertability
title: \textbf{Theorem}
body_md:
\label{Invertability}
For every instance of a logical rule, if its conclusion has a proof of height $n$, then each premise has a proof of height at most $n$.
